g.passage: When the train lurched out of the station at Kollam, Ananya was already watching Radek over the top of her newspaper. Her retired neighbor had insisted on carrying her suitcase, had bought her tea at every stop, and had now offered to hold her ticket while she slept. A sailor, she reminded herself, learns to be charming in every port, and charm usually wants something. She kept the ticket in her fist. Near Alappuzha, however, the conductor came through, and Radek quietly paid the fare difference she had not known she owed, waving off her protest. He explained that her late husband had once done the same for him on a ship bound for Kochi. Ananya folded the newspaper. She found she could not quite meet his eyes, and the tea he handed her next tasted unaccountably sweeter than the last.

g.passage: A brown parcel slid back across the counter, stamped twice in red: REFUSED BY RECIPIENT. Waya read the stamp aloud in the officer's flat voice, and Tallulah laughed despite the fluorescent hum of the Albuquerque checkpoint. Their mother would have called the officer a magistrate of string and tape. They had driven three hours to collect it, sure it held another of her complaints about the price of postage. Tallulah tore it open in the parking lot. Inside, beneath their mother's own letters to her sister, lay a quilt square stitched with the two of them as children, each name embroidered in uneven thread. Waya traced his name with one finger. Neither of them laughed again. They sat in the car with the engine off and read the letters slowly, passing each page back and forth as though it might break.

g.passage:
When the post office opens at eight in Bergen's hills,
Gunnar sorts the letters as he always has,
and Leilani, new this spring, stacks the parcels by weight.
They speak of rain, of the ferry, of the stamp machine's cough.
Neither mentions the empty stool by the window
where the old postmistress kept her thermos warm.
But at noon, when Gunnar pours two cups instead of three,
he pauses with the kettle tilted over nothing,
and Leilani watches the steam drift toward the glass
as if it, too, were waiting for someone to come in.
She slides her own cup toward the window stool
and neither of them says why.

g.passage: What do you owe a friend who has only weeks left? I asked Aiko this on the dock behind her house in Hokkaido, the lake so still that our reflections looked more certain than we did. Ren had asked me, in the hospital, whether his mother had forgiven him, and I had said yes, though she had said nothing of the kind. For days I circled the lie, wondering if I should take it back or let it stand. Aiko, who had known Ren's family for forty years, said only that his mother had sat outside his room every night, unable to go in. I watched a heron lift from the reeds. That evening I went back to the hospital, not to correct myself, but to tell Ren what Aiko had seen, and to let him decide what it meant.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?

g.passage: “I'll need to see the candle receipts again,” Leah said, for the third morning running. I ran the little gift counter at the monastery guesthouse on Chicago's South Side, and by then I could recite her order before she reached the bell. She counted coins slowly, held each receipt to the window, and asked questions no one else bothered to ask. I began greeting her with a smile tight enough to crack. On the fourth morning she laid a twenty-dollar bill on the counter and explained, without any triumph, that I had charged her for a box of candles twice the week before. She had waited, she said, until she was certain, because she did not want to embarrass me in front of the brothers. I took the bill and stared at it a long while. After that, I kept her receipts in a drawer of their own.

seed.conflict: about borrowed money and borrowed time
seed.topicSeed: a seaside promenade in Colombo; a captain and a stowaway about borrowed money and borrowed time

g.passage: How long did a stowaway think a captain's patience could last? Sadia put the question plainly as they walked the promenade in Colombo, the harbor lights behind them. Ayesha had hidden in the cargo hold for six days and now owed passage money she plainly did not have. She offered promises instead: a cousin with a shop, a job by the end of the month, interest on every rupee. Sadia listened without answering. She was remembering a different harbor, twenty years earlier, and a girl curled behind sacks of rice who had been found by a captain far less patient than she was. That captain had put her ashore with nothing. Sadia stopped beside the seawall. She told Ayesha that the debt would keep, and that the month she had mentioned could be two, if the cousin proved slow.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A promise is made, then broken, then bitterly recalled by the captain.
A dispute is described, then settled by an outside figure's decision.
A demand is posed, a memory reframes it, and the demand is eased.
A setting is portrayed at length, then a stranger's past is revealed.
g.explanation: 글은 Sadia가 밀항자 Ayesha에게 인내심의 한계를 묻는 요구로 시작하고, Ayesha의 약속이 이어진다. 중간에 Sadia가 자신도 과거에 밀항했다가 무정한 선장에게 내쫓긴 기억이 나오며, 이 기억이 현재 상황을 다르게 보게 만든다. 결국 Sadia는 빚을 미루고 기한을 늘려 주므로 C가 정답이다. B는 외부 인물이 결정한다고 보지만 결정은 Sadia 자신이 하며, D는 드러나는 과거가 낯선 사람이 아니라 선장 본인의 것임을 놓친다.

g.passage: “I won't be coming to the anniversary dinner,” Bahram said, moving his bishop before Tamar had finished setting the board. They had played on this hillside terrace above Dhaka every Friday for twenty-two years, and for twenty-two years Bahram had won exactly as often as he lost. Tamar had kept a tally in pencil on the underside of the table. He had planned the club's dinner partly to announce the final count. Now he studied his old rival's face and saw, for the first time, a tremor in the hand that held the bishop. Bahram's eyes had been failing for months; he could no longer read a menu, let alone a speech. Tamar said nothing about it. He simply turned the table over, rubbed out the pencil marks with his thumb, and suggested they play on the terrace that night instead.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A competition is recounted, and then its final winner is declared.
A conflict is introduced, and then an apology resolves it at once.
A setting is described, and then a flashback explains the rivalry.
A refusal is stated, and then its hidden cause alters a plan.
g.explanation: 글은 Bahram이 기념 만찬에 가지 않겠다고 거절하는 대사로 시작한다. 이어 두 사람의 오랜 경쟁과 Tamar의 계획이 소개된 뒤, Tamar는 Bahram의 시력이 나빠졌다는 숨은 이유를 알아차린다. 그 결과 Tamar는 기록을 지우고 만찬 대신 테라스에서 두자고 제안하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 최종 승자를 발표하려던 계획을 근거로 한 오답이지만 실제로는 기록이 지워지고, B는 지문에 사과가 없다는 점에서 틀렸다.

g.passage: Some costs are worth paying. I believed this when my mother, Taeyang, and I floated in the salt-water pool on Jeju, arguing over whether my wedding should be small. She wanted a hall for two hundred guests; I wanted the money set aside for my younger cousin's scholarship abroad. My mother let the water hold her and said nothing for a long time. Then she told me about the year she had been offered a place at a university in Seoul and had turned it down so her brother could go instead. She did not regret it, she said, but she had never stopped wondering. I had always thought of sacrifice as a clean exchange, one good traded for another. Watching her stare at the sky, I began to suspect that every such exchange leaves something unpaid.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A belief is stated, tested by a story, and then complicated.

g.passage: Bouzouki music and the clatter of plates filled the wedding hall in Thessaloniki, so loud that no one noticed two guests who had stopped speaking to each other. Zoya had taught Alisha literature for three years, and both of them had come for the bride, Alisha's cousin. An hour earlier, Alisha had handed Zoya an envelope she thought was a thank-you card; inside was a letter Alisha had written to a friend, describing Zoya's lessons with merciless accuracy. Now they sat at opposite ends of the same long table. __When the waiter set down the honey cakes, each of them reached for the plate at the same moment, and each pulled back as if burned.__ Neither moved again until the dancing began. Later, Alisha watched her teacher fold the letter into a small square and tuck it into her purse rather than throw it away.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

g.passage: Karachi's monsoon had softened every page in the bookbinder's workshop, and Savitri, the night nurse, kept a lamp burning beside the narrow bed where old Tomoe slept among his presses. His family visited each afternoon and spoke of him as already gone, discussing which tools to sell. One evening a former apprentice arrived unannounced, a man who had not seen Tomoe in ten years. He stood a long time at the foot of the bed. __Then he pointed to Tomoe's hands, which, even in sleep, were folding the edge of the blanket into careful, even signatures, as if preparing a book for sewing.__ Savitri had seen the motion every night and thought it a restless habit. The apprentice took the bone folder from the bench and placed it gently in the old man's palm, and Tomoe's breathing slowed.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that the apprentice has come to claim the tools.
It explains why the family has decided to sell the workshop.

g.passage: “Smoked eel or herring?” my sister Irena asked, as though I had been gone a week rather than two years. We walked the open-air market in Riga, past Assunta's stall of pickled mushrooms, where Irena had worked every morning while I was at the front. I knew, though she had never written it, that her wages had paid off the loan I took before I left. I had rehearsed a speech of thanks on the train. __At Assunta's stall, Irena paid for both our lunches before I could reach for my wallet, and counted out the coins with the same care she must have used every week I was away.__ I put my hand back in my pocket. We ate on a bench by the canal and talked about the weather, the price of eel, and whether the old tram line would ever reopen.

g.passage: I was fourteen when the rumor about my stepfather climbed the stairwell of our building in Istanbul. Someone on the third floor had decided that he drank, because he came home late and slowly. By the time the story reached our neighbor Yasmin, it had grown into something cruel, and Yasmin told it to the one person who should never have heard it: my mother. I listened from the landing as she repeated it. __My stepfather, coming up behind me with a sack of bread and a bandaged knee from his shift at the docks, stopped on the step below and waited until Yasmin had finished.__ Then he climbed past us, greeted her by name, and went inside to wash his hands. That night my mother unwrapped his knee herself, and I stopped calling him by his first name. I am Eda, I thought, and he is the one who waited.

g.passage: Elan had been certain, for nearly an hour, that Beatriz was the woman who had promised to drive him to Flagstaff. They were the only two adults left in the camp dining hall on the plateau after the bus failed to arrive, and he had greeted her with the confidence of a man reminding someone of a debt. Beatriz, who had never seen him before, listened politely and then admitted she had been just as sure that he was the one who had promised to drive her. Neither had a car. Both had been told, by someone neither could name, that a ride was arranged. Elan considered this with great seriousness, as though the mystery deserved a committee. g.explanation: 서술자는 Elan이 빚을 상기시키는 사람처럼 자신 있게 말했다가 상대도 같은 착각을 했음을 알게 되는 과정을 유머러스하게 그린다. 또한 그가 이 수수께끼를 '위원회가 필요한 일'처럼 진지하게 생각했다고 표현하고, 샌드위치를 나눈 일을 그날 지켜진 유일한 약속이라 부르며 애정을 드러낸다. 따라서 너그럽게 즐거워하는 태도인 B가 정답이다. A는 Elan의 착각을 근거로 한 오답이지만 서술자는 그를 비웃지 않으며, C와 D도 서술자의 따뜻한 어조와 맞지 않는다.

seed.conflict: over an unfair rule everyone obeys
seed.topicSeed: a tailor's back room in Manila; a grandmother and her grandson over an unfair rule everyone obeys

g.passage: Steam hissed from the iron, and the back room of the Manila tailor shop smelled of starch and scorched cotton. Putri had worked there for forty years under the owner's rule that no apprentice could sit while a customer was in the front room, even if the customer was only browsing. Her grandson Kiet, twelve and newly apprenticed, stood for three hours on his first Saturday while a man fingered every bolt of linen and bought nothing. Kiet asked why. Putri said that was simply how it was done. The narrator notes that she had once fainted at the cutting table during such a wait, and that the owner himself had never been seen standing longer than it took to collect the day's money. Yet when Kiet swayed, it was Putri who quietly slid a crate behind his knees, out of sight of the door.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the rule in the tailor shop?
options: Admiring of its strict discipline
Amused by its old-fashioned charm
Critical of it, kind toward Putri
Neutral about it and about the owner
g.explanation: 서술자는 Putri가 기다리다 쓰러진 적이 있고 주인 자신은 돈을 걷는 시간 이상 서 있은 적이 없다고 덧붙여 규칙의 부당함을 드러낸다. 한편 Putri가 몰래 손자의 무릎 뒤에 상자를 밀어 넣는 장면을 보여 주어, 규칙에 따르면서도 손자를 지키는 그녀에게 공감을 보인다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 Putri가 40년간 규칙을 지켜 온 점을 근거로 한 오답이지만 서술자는 이를 칭찬하지 않는다. D는 주인에 대한 비꼬는 서술을 놓친다.

seed.relationship: a father and his stubborn son
seed.conflict: after a competition one of them lost on purpose
seed.topicSeed: a roadside diner in Kingston; a father and his stubborn son after a competition one of them lost on purpose

g.passage:
Kingston's last diner before the highway keeps its coffee hot all night,
and that is where my father, Errol, told me nothing.
He had run the coastal race faster than any man his age,
then slowed in the final mile to let me pass him.
I, Hemi, stubborn as a fence post, wanted him to say it.
He salted his eggs and spoke about the weather.
I hated him a little for the gift, and for the silence,
and for the way he tipped the waitress twice what he could spare,
as if generosity were a habit he could not break.
I keep the medal in a drawer I seldom open.
I am still not sure which of us won.
g.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward his father?
options: Openly grateful for the father's victory
Bitterly certain that the father cheated
Lightly amused by the father's silence
Resentful yet reluctantly admiring
g.explanation: 화자는 아버지가 일부러 져 준 일과 그에 대한 침묵 때문에 아버지를 '조금 미워했다'고 말한다. 동시에 형편보다 두 배의 팁을 남기는 모습을 끊을 수 없는 습관 같은 너그러움으로 묘사하며, 메달을 서랍에 간직하는 데서 마지못한 존경이 드러난다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A는 아버지의 선물을 근거로 한 오답이지만 화자는 고마움을 솔직히 표하지 않고, B는 아버지가 부정행위를 한 것이 아니라 일부러 양보했다는 점을 놓친다.

seed.relationship: a young apprentice and a master carpenter
seed.topicSeed: a salt flat in Tbilisi; a young apprentice and a master carpenter over an old photograph

g.passage: By the end of my first winter as Bogdan's apprentice, I believed there was nothing in wood he could not do. He could hear a crack before it opened and fit a joint so tight that water would not pass. Then one afternoon on the salt flat outside Tbilisi, where we had gone to collect weathered planks, he showed me a photograph of a cabinet he had built at twenty. It leaned slightly to the left. He said he had kept the photograph for fifty years to remember that his hands had once been ignorant. I, Bronislaw, had never imagined him ignorant of anything. I studied the crooked cabinet and felt, oddly, more devoted to him than before. That evening I watched him plane a board and noticed, for the first time, how carefully he checked a measurement twice.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Bogdan?
options: Admiring, and newly aware of his growth
Disappointed, having learned of his flaws
Envious of the talent he was born with
Wary of the secrets he keeps from others
g.explanation: 화자는 처음에 Bogdan이 나무로 못 하는 일이 없다고 믿을 만큼 그를 우러러본다. 스무 살 때 만든 기울어진 장식장 사진을 본 뒤 화자는 실망하기보다 오히려 더 헌신적인 마음을 느끼고, 그가 치수를 두 번 확인하는 모습을 새로 알아차린다. 따라서 존경하면서도 그의 성장 과정을 새롭게 인식했다는 A가 정답이다. B는 결점을 알게 된 상황에서 실망을 예상한 오답이지만 화자는 오히려 더 헌신하게 되며, C는 Bogdan의 실력이 타고난 것이 아니라는 지문 내용과 반대이다.
